ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
National Policy on Land Use 
*281. SHRI PYARELAL KHANDELWAL: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is no national policy on land use in our country; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the soil Management Techniques like nutrient 
buffer power concept are not adequately recognized in the country; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor and how it affects our foodgrain output; 
(d) if not, the details thereof including the details regarding the change of 
agricultural land use; 
(e) whether China has harvested more than 550 million tonnes of foodgrain 
compared to our 200 million tonnes of foodgrain by using above said techniques; 
and 
(f) if so, the comparative study thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to (f) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (f) Land is a State subject. Ministry of Agriculture, had, however, circulated 19 
points National Land Use Policy Outlines (NLPOs) approved by the National Land Use and 
Wastelands Development Council (NLWC) under the Chairmanship of the Prime Minister in 
February, 1986 to States/ UTs for its implementation. It is for the State Land Use Boards 
(SLUBs) to oversee implementation of these action points.  

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2006] 
Agricultural/cultivable land which includes, net sown area, fallow land, 
culturable wasteland land, land under crops and groves has remained more or less 
constant. Agricultural land was 183.63 million ha. in 1998 and the same was 182.92 
million ha. in 2003. During the same period, land under non-agricultural use has increased 
from 22.80 million ha. to 24.25 million ha. This increase in non agricultural land use 
appears to have been met from both cultivable and wastelands. 
Soil fertility evaluation based on nutrient buffer power concept is well 
recognised. Soils in India have also been characterized with respect to this concept. Its 
application in regular soil testing programmes is not, however, very common as the 
technique is complex and cumbersome to follow In this country, a simple, cheap and 
quick method for soil fertility evaluation requiring analysis of large number of soil samples 
is desirable. 
A suitable land use policy plays a role in sustaining crop productivity; various other 
factors like efficiency of production inputs (Soil, Water and Nutrients), minimizing 
production losses caused by pests and weeds, post harvest processing, and handling 
are of even more crucial importance. These aspects are receiving constant attention of the 
Central and State Governments through suitable programmes, and of the National 
Agricultural Research System through researches for improvements in these spheres. 
China's higher food-grain production is attributable to greater use of chemical 
fertilizers (40 million tonnes Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potash against 18 million tonnes in 
India). That country also utilizes higher quantities of organic fertilizer (18 million tonnes 
against 4-6 million tonnes in India). Government of India is promoting the concept of the 
Integrated Nutrient Management to sustain and enhance soil fertility through optimal use of 
chemical and organic nutrients. Another factor for larger foodgrain Deduction in China is 
the higher use of hybrid varieties and higher water prooductivity etc. compared to 
India.

*282. SHRI E. M. SUDARSANA NATCHIPPAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any fresh initiatives have been taken by Government to improve the

7

(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Maintenance of cleanliness and sanitary conditions in Central Government 
Hospitals is always a priority with the Government. Initiatives taken to further improve 
cleanliness levels include: 
(1) Outsourcing of cleanliness and sanitary services in Central Government 
Hospitals in Delhi to private agencies like Sulabh International. 
(2) Undertaking special cleanliness drives with extra staff on weekly/ fortnightly 
basis. 
<3) Installing equipment like, incinerators, microwaves, shredders for handling 
bio-medical waste. 
(4) Segregation of hospital waste through different colour coded bags. 
(5) infection control committees of the hospitals regularly monitor cleanliness 
condditions in hospitals. 
(6) Cleanliness drive is also monitored in specified areas by designated 
officers and also by the Medical Superintendents of the Institution concerned.

Statement 
Development of food processing industries is an ongoing process. Several steps have 
been taken by the Government from time to time for 
13 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2006] 
promotion of the food processing industries in all States including Nagaland. Fruit 
&-vegetable processing units are already exempted from payment of excise duty. In the 
year 2004-05 the Government has allowed under Income Tax Act, a deduction of 
100% of profit for five years and 25% of profits for the next five years in case of new 
agro processing industries set up to process, preserve and package fruits and vegetables.

milk, ice cream, preparation of meat, fish and poultry, pectins, pasta and yeast from

Increasing forest cover 
*285. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have made any comprehensive strategic plan for 
increasing the forest cover by maintaining greenery in the country for the next twenty 
years; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) what steps have been taken or proposed to be taken for increasing 
forest cover in the country; 
(d) the estimated amount to be spent on this plan and whether Government 
have chalked out any plan for the increasing participation of local people in these 
plans; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) to (e) A Statement is 
laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) The National Forestry Action Programme (NFAP) of India 1999 
is a 20 year persective plan for the forestry sector of the 
16 

[10 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
country. The programme document envisaged expansion of forest and tree cover 
by 21.80 million hectares besides regeneration of 26.43 million hectares of 
existing forest area with a proposed total investment of Rs. 133902.78 crores 
in 20 years. 
(c) Following steps have been taken to increase the forest and tree cover in 
the country:— 
(i) Ministry of Environment and Forests is implementing National 
Afforestation Programme (NAP) Scheme for regeneration of 
degraded forests and adjoining forestlands during the Tenth Five Year 
Plan. The Scheme is being implemented through two-tier 
decentralized mechanism of Forest Development Agency (FDA) at 
forest division level and Joint Forest Management Committees (JFMCs) 
at village level. As on 06.02.2006, 680 FDA projects have been 
approved in ail 28 States at a total cost of Rs. 1489.42 crores to cover 
project area of 9.04 lakh hectares through 22,878 JFMCs. 
(ii) Consultation with State Governments and Union Territory (UT) 
administration, including conferences  of Forest Ministers of States 
and Union Territories on 5-6 August, 2004 and 15 February, 2006, 
have been held to sensitize State/UT authorities about the increased 
tree planting targets. 
(iii) State Government and Union Territory Administrations have been 
requested to constitute Chief Secretary-level Committee of all. land 
owning and other concerned Departments to involve them 
in tree planting activities. 
(iv) Guidelines for rationalization of felling and transit regulations for tree 
species grown on non-forest private land have been issued by the 
Ministry of Environment and Forests to the State Governments and 
Union Territory Administrations to encourage private tree plantation. 
(v) State Government and Union Territory Administrations have been 
requested to formulate and implement a comprehensive Media Plan 
to create mass awareness about tree planting. 
(vi) Multi-Stakeholder Partnership (MSP), involving State Forest 
Department, the local village community and the private sector, has 
been mooted for forestation of degraded lands. 
17 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2006] 
 (d) and (e) The NFAP 1999 envisaged a total investment, of Rs. 133902.78 
crore in 20 years. People's participation is considered as an important element of forestry 
sector in the country. The Ministry has issued guidelines dated. 1.6.1990 for involving 
village communities and voluntary agencies for regeneration of degraded forest land 
within conceptual framework of Joint Forest Management (JFM). The Ministry is 
implementing National Afforestation Programme (NAP) during the Tenth Five Year Plan to 
institutionalize and expand JFM. As per information received from States, 99,868 
JFMCs are functioning in all 28 States covering 21.4 million hectares of forest area. An 
allocation of Rs.1205 crores has been provided for NAP during the Tenth Five Year 
Plan.

There are three layers. Through these helplines we try to provide some support and

Strengthening of Public Health Services in Uttaranchal 
*298. SHRI HARISH RAWAT: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any proposal to improve the standard and 
functioning of the Central/State Government hospitals, primary health centres and 
community health centres set up in the rural areas of the country specially in hilly and 
backward areas of Uttaranchal; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) and (b) Under National Rural Health Mission 
(NRHM), it is proposed to provide quality health services through strengthening of 
health infrastructure, adequate and regular supply of essential quality drugs and 
equipment, observance of standard treatment guidelines and protocols. Primary 
Health Centres (PHCs) will be strengthened for 24 hrs. delivery services. The 
Community Health Centres [(CHCs) 30-50 beds] would be operationalised as 24 hours 
First Referral Units (FRUs). CHCs are being upgraded to Indian Public Health Standards 
(IPHS). Manpower requirements of these facilities are also being strengthened. 
Indian Public Health Standards for CHCs have been prepared and shared 
with the States. IPHS for PHCs is under preparation. Rogi Kalyan Samiti/Hospital 
management committee with the involvement of Panchayati Raj Institution are 
being constituted at the PHC, CHC, sub-divisional and district hospitals. Citizen's 
Charter is an important component of IPHS. The states have identified 2 CHCs per 
district for upgradation to Indian Public Health Standards. An amount of Rs. 205 
Crore has been released to the states for such upgradation @ Rs. 20 lakhs per 
CHC for 2 CHCs per district during 2005-06. Rupees 520 lakhs have been 
released to Uttaranchal State for upgradation of 26 CHCs to IPHS. Besides, Rs. 
10,000/- per Sub-centre has been released to the state of Uttaranchal, totalling 
Rs. 1.53 Crores during 2005-06. 
World Bank assisted Health System Development Project with an estimated 
cost of Rs. 77.6 crores is being implemented in the state of Uttaranchal to provide 
quality health care services to rural people, to 
41 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2006] 
provide viable first referral mechanisms i.e. at the level of CHCs, Sub-divisional 
hospitals and district hospitals, to improve the health status of poor and underserved by 
reducing mortality, morbidity and disability and to improve efficiency in allocation and 
use of health resources through policy reform and institutional development. 
Resolution against two-child norm 
*299. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a meeting of the reconstituted National 
Commission on Population was held recently; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that there was a resolution against implementation 
of two-child norm in the country; and 
(c) if so, the reasons for implementing two-child norm by 
Government? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir, the first meeting of the 
reconstituted National Commission on Population was held on 23rd July, 2005, under the 
chairmanship of Hon'ble Prime Minister. Though the issue of two child norm was 
discussed in the meeting, no resolution regarding implementation of the two-child norm in 
the country was adopted by the Commission. In fact, the National Population Policy, 
2000, affirms the commitment of Government towards voluntary and informed choice 
and consent of citizens while availing reproductive health care services and 
continuation of target free approach in administering family planning services. The 
family welfare programme in India is purely voluntary in nature, which enables 
couples to decide the size of their family and adopt the family planning methods, best suited 
to them, according to their choice, without any coersion.

estimated to be varying from 1.79 to 7.14 per cent for foodgrains and pulses

techniques/systems to minimize the losses in agricultural produce in the country

and the All India Coordinated Research Project on Post Harvest Technology. The All 
India Coordinated Research Project on Post Harvest Technology has 33 co-operative

technology packages for crop, livestock product and fisheries produce in terms of 
reducing post harvest losses, aiding value to the main produce and byproducts. 
National Horticulture Board, and autonomous body under this Ministry is 
implementing programmes to reduce post harvest losses by providing investment 
subsidy on the capital cost of infrastructure projects for post-harvest handling, 
processing and marketing of horticulture produce. The rate of subsidy is 20 percent 
of the project cost with a maximum limit of Rs. 25 lakh per project. 
The Department is also implementing schemes for construction/ modernization 
of Cold Storage and Rural godowns in the country with a view to provide scientific 
storage facilities to farmers. Under these schemes, subsidy is provided @ 15 to 25%

Eastern States, hilly areas and Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes entrepreneurs. The

Wastage of agriculture produce 
1946. SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJ EE: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) the percentage of agriculture products wasted during the period 2002-
2005 due to bad quality of seeds and pesticides, year-wise and product-wise; 
and 
(b) the actions being taken by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) and (b) Sir, Seed is the basic input in 
agricultural production system and performance of other inputs is also 
determined by the quality of seeds, which make a difference in production/ 
productivity to the extent of about 45%. In India about 80% seeds used are 
farm saved seeds, which accounts for low seed replacement rate and impacts 
productivity. However, efforts have been made to enhance agricultural 
productivity by promoting use of quality seed. 
The Quality of Seeds is regulated by the Seeds Act, 1966 and Seed 
(Control) Order, 1983, which prescribe minimum seed standards and address 
issues related to production and distribution of seeds. In order to ensure supply 
of quality pesticides to farmers, the Government of India along with State 
Government regulates the import, manufacture, production and sale of 
pesticides under the Insecticides Act, 1968. The Act has sufficient provisions to 
regulate the quality of pesticides distributed to the farmers. Punitive actions are 
taken against the manufacturer/dealer of spurious and misbranded pesticides.

(c) the percentage of Ganges waters being polluted by each and every

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. The 
sources of pollution of river Ganga can be classified broadly into two categories 
namely, point and non-point sources. The point sources are organized source of 
pollution of domestic and industrial origin. The non-point sources are non measurable 
sources of pollution such as run-off from agricultural fields, solid waste dumps and 
areas used for open defecation, dumping of unburnt/half burnt dead bodies 
and animal carcasses, dhobi ghats, cattle wallowing etc. It has been reported that

and industrial wastewater are reported to contribute 75% and 25% of the total 
pollution load respectively caused due to these sources 
(d) An expenditure of Rs. 682.89 crore has already been incurred by the 
Government for undertaking various pollution abatement works in river Ganga since 
1985 till December, 2005. An amount of Rs. 421.99 crore is additionally 
required to take up all other approved pollution abatement works of the river. 
Further, an amount of Rs. 1334 crore approximately has been estimated as the 
requirement to tackle the balance pollution load of the river for improving the river 
water quality to the standard set for bathing class.

counseling and behaviour change communication. Presently 968 
NGOs are implementing 1033 Targeted Interventions across the 
country aiming to prevent HIV transmission among high risk 
groups comprising commercial sex workers, injecting drug users, 
men having sex with men, migrant labors, truckers and street

package of services including behavior change communication, 
treatment of sexually transmitted infections, linkage for care and 
support

services, condom promotion and enabling environment for behavior

blood safety, voluntary counseling and testing services, Prevention of Parent to

(IEC). To prevent the spread of HIV infection amongst adolescents, 
National Action Plan has been developed for HIV Prevention Education to 
reach 100% secondary and senior secondary schools under Adolescent 
Education Programme. The programme aims to provide information on 
HIV transmission and prevention, development of life skills and 
reinforcing existing positive behavior among students, promote abstinence

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) According to Indian 
Council of Medical Research, hepatitis B infection is several times more infectious 
than AIDS. 
Hepatitis B spreads through unsafe sex, unsafe blood transfusion, unsafe injection 
etc. and also from mother to child. Hepatitis B is preventable by ensuring 
precautionary measures. The Government has launched a pilot project of immunization 
of Hepatitis B free of cost for children below one year only. Hepatitis B vaccination has 
commenced and is continuing in 15 cities since 2002-03 and in 32 districts and 
Andaman and Nicobar Island since 2003-04. 
While the general health care delivery system in the country is well equipped to 
handle various diseases, Hepatitis B is effectively tackled through preventive 
measures including vaccination. The following measures have been taken to prevent 
infection of Hepatitis B:— 
• Central Government Hospitals personnel at high risk are being immunized 
against Hepatitis B. State Governments have also been advised to take 
similar steps. 
• Guidelines have been issued for mandatory testing of blood in blood banks. 
• Promotion of safe sex under National AIDS Control Programme is advocated. 
• Health awareness campaigns regarding dangers of using non-sterile syringes 
and needless under National AIDS Control Programme are held.

a specific medical devices division for their regulation. The Committee has also 
recommended for an appropriate regulatory mechanism to be set up under Central Drug 
Authority for certification, quality assurance and post marketing surveillance of imported as 
well as locally made medical devices. A Committee under DDG(M) has been to go into 
these recommendations and suggest appropriate legislation. In the mean time 10 sterile 
medical devices which are of critical nature, have been notified. By the Government under 
Section 3(b)(iv) of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act in order to ensure appropriate 
regulation over their import and manufacture.

2041. SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TA IMUR: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that most of the drugs used to treat new-born babies 
have not been properly tested, even some drugs like morphine, thyrozine and 
some anti-epileptic drugs are unlicensed for use of children; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
171 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2006] 
(c) whether Government have issued any instructions to the 
pharmaceutical companies to test and certify all paediatric medicines; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) 
Generally, the clinical trial at various phases during the course of 
development of a new drug is conducted on adult patient population because 
of difficulty in undertaking trials on children. However, depending upon the 
safety profile, the paediatricians may us e these drugs for treatment of various 
diseases and disorders in children in recommended paediatric doses, unless 
during the market authorization, there is  any specific restriction for use of a 
drug in children. 
As per the standard texts and medical literature, drugs like morphine, 
thyrozine (thyroxine) and most of anti-epileptic drugs are also being used in 
children. 
(c) and (d) The Schedule Y to Drugs  and Cosmetics Rules, which was 
amended in January 2005 provides that if a new drug has a potential for use in 
paediatric patients, paediatric safety study should be conducted. In cases where 
there is limited paediatric data at the time of submission of application, more 
data in paediatric patients would be expected after marketing authorization for 
use in children is granted.

New AIDS treatment by German scientists 
2048. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that German scientists have developed a new 
treatment for HIV, which is useful in targeted, mutated strains of AIDS virus 
that they become impervious to drugs; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that they succeeded in blocking the 
multiplication of HIV-l; 
(c) if so, the details of the research; and 
(d) what is the difference between the conventional therapies and the latest 
discovery which neutralized the human protein? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Yes, Sir. It is a 
fact that a team of German scientists from the Heinrich Pette Institute in Hamburg 
and Nuremberg-Eriangen University, led by llona Hauber, announced in January 
2005 that they had developed a new treatment of HIV that is useful in targeted 
mutated strains of the AIDS virus that have become impervious to drugs. The scientific 
article explaining their research appeared in the "Journal of Clinical Investigations" 
published from the US, in January, 2005. 
(b) It is claimed that they have succeeded in blocking the multiplication 
of HIV-1, including those strains of the virus that have developed resistance 
against all currently available anti-retroviral drugs. 
177 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2006] 
(c) A human cellular protein called 'hypusine' is necessary for HIV 
replication, Hypusine synthesis is facilitated by a human cellular protein 
called 'deoxyhypusine synthase' (DHS). The investigators identified a 
substance called guanylhydrazone CNI-1493 as an efficient inhibitor of 
human DHS. By inhibiting DHS, this compound suppresses Hypusine 
formation and, thereby HI V multiplication. Further, the investigators also 
claimed that no measurable drug-indu ced adverse effects were observed. 
However, results of further trials are awaited. 
(d) Conventional therapies, usi ng the currently available anti- 
retrovira! drugs, target viral proteins called gp41, Reverse Transcriptase 
and Protease, which are essential for the entry of the virus into human 
CD4 cell and its multiplication ther e. The newly identified CNI-1493,on 
the other hand, targets a human protein called deoxyhypusine synthase 
(DHS), which is also essential for multiplication. Since HIV resistance is 
against currently used drugs that inhibit the synthesis of viral proteins 
only, the new drug effectively inhibits the synthesis of viral proteins only, 
the new drug effectively inhibits the multiplication of resistant strains also.

Losses due to delay of Trains 
†2069. SHRI SHATRUGHAN SINHA Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Railways have to bear heavy losses due to delayed running of 
trains; 
(b) the other reasons for delayed running of trains besides natural problems 
such as fog and agitations; and 
(c) the steps taken to ensure timely running of trains? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI R. 
VELU): (a) Delayed running of trains increases the transit time apart from causing 
dislocation to the paths of other trains. However, the overall losses incurred by the 
Railways due to delayed running of trains are not computed and only in specific cases 
viz., breaches, flood etc. when a considerable disruption to through traffic is caused are the 
losses computed for the given period. 
(b) The other reasons for late running of trains on Indian Railways besides fog & 
agitations are accidents, bundhs, bad weather, alarm chain pulling, miscreant activities, signal 
failures, over head equipment failures, loco failures, cattle run over, grid failures, human 
failures etc. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
192 

[10 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) The following steps are taken by Indian Railways to improve operations 
and the punctuality of passenger carrying trains; 
(1) Intensive, round the clock monitoring of trains at all three levels viz. 
Divisional, Zonal Head Quarters and Railway Board. 
(2) Punctuality drives are being conducted from time to time. 
(3) Running of trains at maximum permissible speed subject to observance of 
safety limits and speed restrictions. 
(4) Improvements in Time tabling to provide a clear path. 
(5) Improvement in standard of maintenance of assets to reduce equipment 
failures. 
(6) Counseling and motivating staff to ensure punctual running. 
(7) Liaison with state Government to tackle the Law and Order problems 
and miscreant activities. 
(8) Up-gradation of technology of track, rolling stock and signaling. 
(9) To further strengthen the monitoring of punctuality, introduction of Coaching 
Operations Information System (COIS) has been introduced.

THE BUDGET (GENERAL), 2006-2007 • Contd. 
SHRI ARJUN KUMAR SENGUPTA (West Bengal): Mr. Deputy 
Chairman, Sir, thank you very much for giving me an opportunity to speak on 
this occasion. I am not a politician. I normally do not speak on every occasion. 
I hope, this time, you will allow me to speak at length because the subject, 
under discussion, is very important. I must say: Whether this Budget is 
outstanding or not, does not depend on t he Prime Minister's certificate. It 
depends on a very critical analysis of wh at the Budget provides for, what the 
Budget has failed to provide, and what we expect from the Budget. And, this 
applies not only to the Members of the Congress Party, the UPA, but also to 
the BJP, the NDA side. 
Yesterday, Shri Yashwant Sinha made a very major speech, and the 
speech should be responded to. I wish I had time to respond to his very 
detailed remarks, almost like an account ant. And, I think, somebody from the 
Government should be able to do that. But I will take up a few issues, which 
he had raised, within the limited time that you have given me. I must admit that 
Shri Yashwant Sinha is country's one of the very famous reformers. There is 
no doubt about it. As a Finance Minister, I think, we should admit, he was the 
original reformer. But the only problem is that he keeps a wrong company. His 
first Budget - which he prepared, before Dr. Manmohan Singh's Budget, I 
happened to have seen that, many of us have seen that -- was a unique 
Budget. That was the first original reform Budget. Unfortunately, he was, at 
that time, keeping the company of Shri Chandra Sekhar, and could not 
present the Budget.  And, then, later, 
222 

[10 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
he presented a number of Budgets, which were full of reforms. But 
unfortunately, because of the company that he was keeping, he came to be 
known as a flip-flop Finance Minister. He proposed something, withdrew that 
something. And, this is totally oppos ed to any notion of reforms. The first 
principle of reforms is that you must be consistent so that people in the 
country, investors, consumers, producers,  know that there is a stability of 
policy, then, you can, actually, get into the details of the policy. 
Mr. P. Chidambaram has shown in th is Budget that he is consistent. 
I must say that this House must compliment him for sticking to the main 
principles of reforms that he initiate d. He did not introduce any changes in 
taxes and other measures. I know the Pink Press is not very happy. They 
expect a big bang reform every year, but that is not reform. The reforms he 
has produced, he kept to that and he has told the world that he is sticking to 
these reforms. The result of that has been felt in several instruments for 
economic change. I don't want to get into the discussions of growth because 
that is the outcome of ma ny unpredictable features. Ev en then, it is perfectly 
possible for Mr. P. Chidambaram to claim that his Government has performed 
much better than the previous Government's growth records, which we 
discussed earlier. But, growth, ultimately, depends on many tilings. What 
reforms should do is to talk about the specific instru ments, which are 
controlling the country's future and country's prospects. What are those 
elements? Those elements are: investment , savings, revenue, fiscal deficit, 
and all these issues. Mr, P. Chidambaram's record has been enormous in 
that. I come to this point first, raising an issue with Mr. Yashwant Sinha. He 
says that this Budget does not have a strategy. I am surprised. This is the first 
Budget which has clearly spelt out a stra tegy. The strategy is that we shall 
continue to do reforms, we shall continue to have economic growth, we shall 
continue to have fiscal discipline, but we shall serve the main objectives of the 
Common Minimum Programme. 
Sir, all reforms are instruments; they are not objectives. Objectives 
are, actually, suppressed. Objectives  maybe increase disparities, and 
objective maybe to have a 'Shining India'; only a few people would be 
enjoying, the rest of the country would suffer. These are the possible 
objectives. Mr. P. Chidambaram becomi ng the Finance Minister of the UPA 
Government, 'which Mr. Yashwant Sinha has described as Chidambaram 
Mark-ll, Chidambaram Mark-ll has expre ssed, categorically, that his reform is 
aimed primarily to achieve the objectives of the UPA Government.   What 
223 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2006] 
are those reforms? Welfare of aam admi, rural employment, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, 
Mid-Day-Meal scheme, drinking water, sanitation, rural health mission, urban 
renewal, child development, Bharat Nirman for irrigation, rural water supply, rural 
roads, rural housing, and rural electrification. Large increase in allocation has been 
given to all these items. He, categorically, states that his Budget is aimed to serve 
this purpose. I want to put this point also to my Left friends. This is the first time, 
categorically, a Budget is saying something that this Budget is aimed at the benefits 
of the poor, benefits of the common people, and he must be complimented for that. 
This is the strategy which Mr. Yashwant Sinha has missed out because the result of 
their policies has been just the reverse. It increased disparity, it increased these 
differences, this 'Shining India" part -II etc. and all these have been the result of 
those policies. They would not consider taking these out openly as objectives, 
though these objectives are suppressed in their actual policies. Mr. Yashwant Sinha 
has just left He seemed to be very unhappy that Mr. P. Chidambaram talked about 
and has taken credit for increase, in the rate of savings and the rate of investment. 
Those of you who were here yesterday must have heard very detailed description of this 
particular issue. Investments and savings are major instruments of policy, and, it is a 
fact that in our country investments and savings have increased very substantially, 
particularly, over the last two, three years. I would submit to you that Mr. 
Chidambaram has every reason to take credit for this. Mr. Yashwant Sinha 
mentioned that why you are taking credit for rising savings. Mr. Deputy Chairman, 
let me put forward this question very ca tegorically. There are three elements of 
savings - household savings, public sector savings and corporate sector savings. 
As regards the household savings, Mr. Sinha was eloquent in saying that in their 
time, household savings had increased. Unfortunately, household savings are least 
responsive to economic policy. If the income increases, savings also increase, 
because the marginal rate of savings is positive. People save more when they 
earn more. It does not depend much upon any policy. And, it so ha ppened that 
during these years we have sustained economic growth; therefore, there would be 
more savings quite automatically. 
The second factor is demography. Because, in India, the major proportion 
of our population Is young; therefore, the rate of savings would be high. This is 
exactly what happened in Japan, this is exactly what happened in many parts of 
the world where the rate of savings went up and also where the rate of savings went 
down when the proportion of their older   people increased.   Young people 
save more, the old less. So, I 
224 

[10 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
submit that on household savings, there is little that the Government can take 
credit, except saying just statistically that household savings had also increased 
during the NDA period. It has increased in the period of Mr. Chidambaram also. 
Mr. Sinha took a lot of credit, on that which does not really belong to him. But 
they take the other two elements also . public sector and corporate sector 
savings. The private corporate savings has been around four per cent, for quite 
some time. As a matter of fact, during the NDA period it, actually, came down 
slightly, but then, with this new Government, corporate savings have also increased 
marginally. I won't take much credit for that. This is also a part of the growth. 
But, if there is a credit that has to be taken, it has to be taken because of the 
policies which affect private corporate sector. What about public savings? Public 
savings constitute two parts - public enterprises and the Government savings. Now, 
as regards the public enterprises, many of our friends, particularly, on the other 
side, decry public sector all the time. The public sector's contribution to national 
savings has been very high, comparable to private corporate sector, if not more. 
It is* 4.5 to 4.8 per cent, and it has been consistent. But, what has happened 
is, during the NDA period, the Government dissavings were so high that the 
public savings part came negative. Let me give you the figures. In 1999-2000, 
public savings were -0.9; in 2000-2001, -1.8; in 2001-02,-2.0; in 2002-03,-0.7. it 
slightly increased In the next year, during the other Finance Minister, Shri Jaswant 
Singh's Budget. Then, last year, it went to 2.2. This is because the 
Government's dissavings were under control. During the previous period, the 
Government's dissavings went rampant; therefore, the public savings rate went 
down. So, the credit for this current increase naturally, goes to Mr. Chidambaram. 
The next question is investment. Mr. Yashwant Sinha was very unhappy 
that Mr. Chidambaram is taking credit for increase in investment. Unfortunately, 
again, for Mr. Yashwant Sinha, the statisti cs show that the rate of investment 
was going down during the period when he was the Finance Minister, and, it 
has only recently moved up. The most important thing is that the private 
investment rate earlier came down. For public investment, you can have your 
Government's own decision. Even if you are not expecting profit, you can go on 
investing. But the private investment is entirely dependent upon your confidence 
with the Government's policies, because you are talking about future. If you do not 
have confidence in your Government's policy, you do not invest. You do not 
know how the economy is going to behave, and that is exactly what happened. 
The private investment went down steadily.  The growth of private investment 
became 
225  

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2006] 
negative during the  NDA period, and it has again moved up now. Therefore, I 
submit, Mr. Chidambaram very legitimately claims credit for that. 
Then, Mr. Yashwant Sinha talks about the overall picture and inflation. 
Now, I just want to dwell on it a little because I don't think we should spend much 
time on that now. Inflation is again not a question of just an increase in price for 
one shot. It is true, and he has referred to the aspect of the petroleum price 
increase. And, I submit that the petroleum price increases must be allowed to be 
passed on. My Left friends are totally mistaken on that. You cannot suppress this 
possibility, the importance of Increase in petroleum prices. Mr. Chidambaram does 
not have to wait for the Rangarajan Committee. In fact, during his previous 
Finance Ministership, he had accepted -- there was a Cabinet decision -- that 
increases in oil prices will be passed on. Because if it is not passed on, --and this is 
what my Left friends must realise -• it affects only the health of the public sector 
enterprises. You cannot do without that. Somebody will have to pay for this. The 
Government cannot pay for this. The total amount of the deficit would be so 
high. So, it is the public enterprises which have to bear this burden. This 
happened earlier. For a long period, there was a huge bill that came to the public 
enterprises, and at that time the decision was taken, after the Oil Bonds were 
floated, that this would be passed on to the public. This decision does not require 
any further examination. It is a political decision. We have to allow this increase in 
prices to pass on. You may have to do some calibration for kerosene or LPG 
because that affects a lot of poor people, but nothing more than calibration. This 
has to be actually increased. 
I want to put forward another point about interest rate that has been 
talked out. Mr. Yashwant Sinha is very worried that interest rates are firming up, and 
he has reasons to worry; if interest rates firm up, it is quite possible that there would 
be some problem. But, again, the international environment is towards raising the 
interest rate and, therefore, we should be worried. But if we control the public 
borrowing, if the deficit of the Government comes down, that will have a signal 
effect on the control of interest rate. And, there is also a question of management. 
Fortunately, during Mr. Yashwant Sinha's time, we had a Governor of Reserve Bank, 
my friend, Bimal Jalan, who managed the interest rates in such a way that it could 
be controlled. But this is a fact -- that should be noted -- that if you control your rate 
of fiscal deficit, it itself will have an effect on interest rate. 
226 

[10 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
So, why is Mr. Yashwant Sinha so suddenly worried about interest rate is not very 
clear to me. 
Now, I come to the question of fiscal deficit. It seems - and this is a very 
major point that you must realise -- that Mr. Chidambaram considers that the crucial 
element of his reform programme is fiscal discipline. He is saying, "Yes, we shall do 
expenditures, investment in different places with growth, but the fiscal discipline 
has to be maintained." Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I think this is the most important 
and very correct decision in a country where fiscal profligacy is a very common thing. I 
heard yesterday Shrimati Brinda Karat saying, 'We opposed this fiscal FRBM Act." 
I am sorry, this should not be opposed because this is a restriction that you are 
putting on to yourself, how to meet all the requirements within your Budget. Why is it 
so? You need to control that. It is not a question of inflation; it is a question of 
with drawing resources from the private sector, and the private sector is very 
important. The crowding-out effect is very important. You may not like the 
corporate sector making profit, but the corporate sector is a major element in our 
economy, and if you create a situation wherein they lose their confidence, lose their 
investment potential, then it would arrest your rate of growth. 
Now, Sir, I come to the fiscal deficit target. For that, Mr. Chidambaram 
has put maximum emphasis on revenue deficit, which is the correct thing. The 
revenue deficit is coming down. In fact, he has shown, in spite of the pause he has 
talked about, that he has been able to stick to the particular discipline, that current 
expenditure must be reduced. You c annot finance current expenditure by 
borrowing. 
There is a point, which I should admit, my friends, Shrimati Brinda Karat 
and others may be right about that there is no need to make a fetish of a particular 
figure, particularly when the country is growing at 8 per cent. It is not necessary that 
you have to make three or three-and-a-half per cent fiscal deficit to be the only thing, 
because it is possible when necessary to go up a little bit. But that is only when 
necessary, when you don't have money to meet all your programmes, that you 
may go in for this kind of fiscal deficit, and a little bit more than that. 
Sir, Mr. Chidambaram has made a statement, which I think is a bit 
awkward. He says that he is very happy to know that gross Plan expenditure is 
now less than the fiscal deficit. So, he is saying that we are not financing the Plan 
expenditure entirely by borrowing. It only means that 
227 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2006] 
there Is a scope for increased borrowing, because if Plan expenditures cannot 
be sustained by borrowing, then nothing can be sustained by borrowing. But 
what I find most interesting in this Budget is that Mr Chidambaram has been able 
to meet the requirements of Plan, increase the Plan expenditure, without entering 
into a major fiscal deficit, or revenue deficit. 
Sir, I would like to make one final point. Here again, I wish to address 
my Left friends in particular; I don't know whether they are listening to me. The 
amount of allocations for the social sector is so substantial that we have to be 
very careful about what happens to that  money. We must think before we say 
that more money should be given to that. In fact, towards everything you could 
give more money. In our country, there is no limit to the absorptive capacity of the 
system of expenditure. But before you do that, you must be able to say whether 
we are spending the money correctly. Here, I find that there is a major problem 
in this country. It is not so much his responsibility that he must take that into 
account, because it has been touched upon in the Congress's Vision Document, in 
the Common Minimum Programme. This is the question of concurrent evaluation. 
There must be a mechanism by which he should be able to see that the money 
that is being spent is actually going to the people. The original bureaucratic way of 
looking at It, of looking into whether  money has been spent, by way of a 
utilisation certificate, is not enough. We have to have mechanisms to see who is 
responsible, how the responsibility is being carried out, whether the actual 
outcomes in terms of delivery have taken place, and where Panchayats, NGOs 
and everybody else will have to be brought together. 
Sir, I submit that Mr. Chidam baram might set up a mechanism. Of 
course, he cannot set ft up on his own; the Prime Minister will have to set it up; he 
sets up Group of Ministers. Many GoMs, half-a-dozen or dozen GoMs, have 
been set up. But this particular GoM,  with the Finance Minister, Planning 
Commission, Panchayati Raj, Rural Development Ministry, should immediately 
work out a programme of concurrent evaluation of this expenditure. This is very 
important. Because, we have raised expectations in the country that this will be 
done. 
Sir, enormous things have been don e on the Rural Employment 
Guarantee Scheme. I am afraid, not everybody realises the implications of that. 
This is the 'rights' approach. We have been able to tell the people, 'you have a 
right to ask for employment'. Then, that employment has to be provided. Now if 
we do not provide that, if we create an expectation and

then that expectation is not fulfilled, I am  sorry, the system is at the point of 
explosion and all of us play a role in that particular development. 
Sir, now I come to my final point. Mrs. Brinda Karat was right that on the 
front of agriculture, the Finance Minister should have done much more. It is true 
that the agriculture growth is only 2.5 per cent. Brinda was absolutely right that we 
are not going to reach the target of four per cent growth and we have to spend a 
lot of time and exercise to do something necessary for that purpose. I felt a little 
bad when I heard that in the Budget Mr.  Chidambaram has referred to another 
committee which will be formed to see as to how the credit can actually go to 
the marginal and small farmers. It is not necessary. Last year, the Committee 
on Rural Credit under Prof. Vyas - a very famous economist who has got Padma 
Bhushan -- has given out its report that spells out as to what should be done to 
improve the credit delivery to the marginal sector. We do not need anything more 
than that. (Time-bell) 
Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I beg to submit that today what is 
necessary is that we should live up to  the promises that we make. Mr. 
Chidambaram has come out with a clear strategy, has given a Budget which 
has a direction, which has a commitment. I only hope that he lives up to the 
expectations of the people. I thank you for having given me the opportunity to 
participate in this discussion.

SHRI LALIT SURI (Uttar Pradesh): Hon. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I am thankful to 
you for giving me time to express my views on the General Budget 2006-2007, 
presented by the Finance Minister on 28th February, 2006. Being from the corporate 
world, I would restrict myself to the core areas of the Budget. Never before has India 
witnessed an upbeat mood; some chose to call it 'India Shining' and others call it 
'India Everywhere'. The fact, however, remains that India is now on the move. India's 
economic growth is being globally recognised. The emergence of India as a global 
economic giant is becoming an accomplished fact. It is your responsibility, Mr. Finance 
Minister, to accelerate this growth process, and it is our responsibility, as 
Parliamentarians to help you to do that. Democracy must become an enabling 
factor in wealth creation. Democracy cannot become a roadblock. 
Let us analyse the parameters of India's economic growth. Our service 
sector and manufacturing sector are both growing up over nine per cent annually. Our 
agriculture sector is still nature dependent. Even though we touched the figure of 215 
million tonnes of foodgrains production once, we have not been able to break the 
hump. Indian growth process has to percolate down. For this, it is necessary that 
agricultural growth hasten, prosperity is evident even amongst the weaker sections 
and those in rural India, who comprise over 60 per cent of India's population, have a 
larger share in GDP contribution than the meagre 22 per cent that becomes the 
basis of inequality. To have a GDP growth rate of 10 per cent, agriculture must 
grow at the rate of four per cent. 
Sir, the key to resolution of India's economic problems lies in rapid 
expansion of the manufacturing sector. The first industrial revolution bypassed. 
India's history has provided us with a second opportunity to 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2006] 
grow. It is manufacturing which creates jobs; it is manufacturing which absorbs 
youth from rural India and counters the under employment in agriculture. It is 
manufacturing which enables revenue collection. It is this revenue collection, which 
accelerates infrastructure development, it is the responsibility of the Government to 
enable the manufacturing sector to grow and grow rapidly. 
The growth of India's manufacturing sector has been entrepreneur-driven and 
not policy-driven. The Government may take satisfaction in the 9 per cent growth in 
the manufacturing sector but this is far below our potential. The growth of 
manufacturing countries like China achieved a rate of annual growth between 12-15 
percent; that became the engine of growth. How our 9 per cent growth transforms itself 
into 15 per cent manufacturing growth? Where we are lacking? Lacking from our 
competitors. Our competitors are no longer high-cost economies. The high cost 
economies are becoming rapidly non-competitive in manufacturing, particularly in the 
low-end economy. Their salary structures, their labour cost, their cost of immovable 
properly, the cost of maintaining envir onment are exorbitant. They can never 
compete with low cost economies. 
What are the steps required to increase India's competitive edge? First, the 
industry needs capital on internationally competitive rate of interest. If the cost of capital 
is 5 per cent more than our competitors, our products are bound to cost more. I 
see a disturbing trend of increase in the borrowing rates in the last two years. This 
has a tendency to make our manufacturing sector become non-competitive. The 
Finance Minister ought to address this question immediately. Manufacturing industry 
must grow at 12 per cent to have a GDP of 10 per cent. It is only 8 per cent to 10 
per cent growth rate, which can eradicate the curse of poverty from the face of India. 
Today, the welfare of the country lies in generation of wealth and its distribution to the 
people. Reducing the Excise Duty on small cars is a very good step, which will one 
day make India as one of the leading exporters of small cars all over the world. 
Secondly, our Infrastructure needs to be globally competitive. The National 
Highway Development Programme and the Rural Roads Programme are 
commendable. They need to be accelerated. Our ports are clogged. This reduces 
our efficiency. The privatization of ports, particularly the container berths in the JNPT 
Port, the Chennai Port and the Tuticorin Port are huge success stories. Privatization 
of ports is a good process. The Government must be proud of it and not 
apologetic. 
244 

[10 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
Thirdly, the cost of utilities and the availability of power have to be 
rapidly addressed. If the cost and avai lability of power make our industry non-
competitive, the country pays a price for it. The Finance Minister has paid 
special attention to the power sector by announcing five 5000 MW coal based 
power plants to be built in the next fi ve years. I would request the Finance 
Minister that stringent conditions should be applicable to the companies which 
are setting up these power plants so that they are totally time-bound. 
The incentives available in the Income Tax Act on private investment 
in infrastructure under section 10(23G) have been removed in the present 
Budget. This is a disturbing trend. I app eal to the Finance Minister to have a 
re-look at this. 
On the front of labour law reforms, India does not need lethargic and 
non-competitive establishments. India needs an efficient economy comprising 
of efficient industrial units, which cr eate more jobs rather than lose them. 
Conservative Labour law regime that exists in India today is actually anti-
labour. It prevents the creation of more  jobs and prevent saving the existing 
ones. It is only efficient economy that cr eates job. The conservative labour 
law regime prevents that. It is a slew of  measures in this direction, which 
actually can enable a faster acceleration of our manufacturing sector. The 
rationalization of duties, the lowering of tariffs is an area where successive 
Governments, including the present Finance Minister, deserve to be 
congratulated. What is important? India is hardl y having consumer goods; 
most of it are capital goods and raw material, which are otherwise not 
available here. A higher duty structure will increase input costs. Lower duty 
structure control the input costs and make the sector more competitive. The 
growth in the present Budget is welcome. 
The Finance Minister must remember that India's economy in the last 
three years has grown by 8.4 per ce nt, 7.5 per cent and 8.1 per cent 
(estimated). How many countries in the world witnessed a continuous growth 
rate of an average of 8 per cent in the last 3 years? Over the next few years, 
we visualize the same growth rate. Should not the environment created by 
this 8 per cent growth rate made the Finance Minister bolder? Sir, your real 
test will not be how many Budgets you present. The real test will be the 
contents of those Budgets. You will be tested by the footprints you leave 
behind. I can understand the compulsions of coalition politi cs, but coalition 
politics are created not for making political points. They are created for 
serving the country. My friends in the Left Parties would do well to help 
245 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2006] 
the UPA Government from onerous conservatism and allow them to achieve a 
growth rate of 10 per cent in a similar manner they are moving in liberalization 
direction in West Bengal, let them have this process also in New Delhi. 
Sir, On the Services sector, we must remember that the bulk of 
India's GDP is contributed by Services. Today 54% of GDP comes from 
services. Ours is an over populated country. We do not visualize the 
population stabilization over the next two decades. We have surplus manpower. 
How do we leverage the liability of population into a national advantage? The world 
today is suffering from demographic misbalance. Population of several 
countries is decreasing. They need m en to man their economies. We have 
surplus manpower; from brain-drain ou r status has now shifted to a brain-
bank. We must, therefore, unleash this energy to the advantage of our country 
and allow this country to dominate the world. Infrastructure never creates 
hurdles in the growth of the service sector. If at all the hurdles are smaller, that 
is why our infrastructure grows. We need to continue to expand the base of 
our education which will enable us to grow in the service sector. Any opening 
out in the service sector will be to our advantage. If China is the manufacturing 
hub of the world, the services by India, the Indian brand is a global leader. The 
policy of the Government has thus to be to give an impetus to the service 
sector. The Finance Minister has been a little harsh in including a larger 
number of services within the service tax net. He has also increased the rate 
of the service tax. The Revenue Secretary will always advice the Revenue 
Minister to generate the area of more taxes. The Finance Minister should make 
sure that this increase in taxes, in cluding wider net for service taxes, may 
adversely affect the service industry an d actually provide him lesser taxes. 
Cheaper services, lesser taxes on services will enable services to grow. 
My own experience of tourism compels me to say that high rates of 
taxation by State Governments coupled with service tax is making hotel room 
rates in India globally non-competitive. The rooms are booked not because our 
rooms are competitive but because there is shortage of rooms. 11 % of global 
population gets employment through tourism. In a country like ours, we have only 
92,000 rooms and require at least 1,00,000 more rooms immediately with an 
investment of Rs.75,000 crores. Our neighbouring countries like Dubai, 
Indonesia, Thailand, Sri Lanka, Malaysia, though much smaller in size, have 
substantially more rooms than what we have in India. Last year 3.9 million 
tourists visited India whereas 45 million in China. The 
246 

[10 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
tourism industry in China earns US$ 95 billion whereas we earn US$ 5.5 billion. 
India has mountains, beaches, religious and cultural centres, the forests, the cities 
and deserts to attract all this. No country in the world can offer what India can offer 
for tourism. It is a twelve-month tourism hub. Being bigger generator of 
employment, it provides 17 million jobs directly and 25 million jobs indirectly. At the 
present growth rate, by year 2010, it will create another 25 million jobs. We need 
infrastructure support. We require larger airports, we need more planes, cleaner 
trains, excellent transport services and, above all, we need cheaper room rates that 
will come only when land rates are lower and taxes are reasonable. What disturbs 
me is not the quality of our hotels. We are almost better than the best. But where is 
the expansion of the hotel rooms, particularly in 3-Star category, taking place? It is 
because of the land rates. This expansion of moderately costly hotel rooms, which 
will enable volumes of hotels to grow, is moving at a very slow pace. This has 
neither received the attention of the Central or the State Governments. My 
suggestion is that the Finance Minister should provide full infrastructure status and 
various incentives to the Tourism industry as is being availed by other industries like 
ports, airports, highways, information technology and telecommunication. I appeal to 
the Finance Minister to look into this. As stated in my last budget speech, I have 
always been a firm believer and advocate of liberalization and disinvestments. It is 
very disheartening to see that the pace of disinvestments has slowed down which is 
detriment to the growth of economy. With Dr. Manmohan Singh, the Prime Minister 
of the country and the architect of liberalization and disinvestments, along with the 
Finance Minister and Mr. Montek Singh Ahluwalia, the Vice-Chairman of Planning 
Commission, the country couldn't have asked for more. To take full advantage of the 
present growth rate in India and to accelerate it further, the Finance Minister must 
increase the pace of disinvestments. Le ft Parties, their allies in the UPA 
government, have already started the process of disinvestments in West Bengal, 
which might even leave the Central Government behind. 
Sir, I have already said, your budget could have been bolder on the 8% 
growth rate, which has enabled direct taxes to grow by 34%. Even indirect taxes 
have grown by 12%. This year's Finance BilI contains as many as 29 amendments 
having retrospective effect like section 43B, 234A, 234B, 234C, 14A of the Act. On the 
MAT, the Laffer curve impact is most visible in the case of direct taxes. Over the last 
ten years the Tax GDP ratio has gone up from 1.3% to 3.4% in the case of 
corporate taxes and from 1.1% Into 2% in the case of Income Tax. These are few of 
the 29 amendments, which

I would like the Finance Minister to look into, When volumes of taxes are going up, 
where is the need to impose more taxes on the people? Higher growth rate, greater 
economic activity, larger revenue collection is a recipe for relief not for higher 
taxation. Your dream budget of 1996 was a huge step in tax rationalization. This 
has to be extracted for an annual 10% growth rate. An 8% growth rate is not 
merely a revenue collection exercise it must ensure prosperity, wealth creation, 
Government enrichment and the greatest good for the greatest number. It must bring 
relief and not onerous obligation. 
With these words, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I support the Budget and 
hope that the hon. Finance Minister will give due consideration to my suggestions. 
Thank you.

thing is failure of credit. He is in a debt  trap. He is not able to get credit when 
needed at easy terms, at easy rate of interest and he has to take it from 
moneylenders. When the time comes, the moneylenders will get back the 
money at their cost.   He knows that he has to pay them back. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI DATTA MEGHE) in the Chair] 
And, ultimately, it is failure of the Government, it may be the present 
Government or the previous Governme nt, but the Government machinery at 
the level of politicians as well as bureaucrats has failed the farmer. So, these 
four factors - failure of water, failure  of seeds, pesticides, and insecticides, 
failure of credit and failure of Government machinery have led to his plight and 
really his tale is a tale of woes and a tale of tears. He is born in debt, he lives 
in debt, and he dies in debt. Something has to be done about it. If it is not 
done and fundamental factors are not looked into, then suicides will get 
continuing, whatever kind of development activities you might do. Death is not 
because of starvation. I come from Ra jasthan, a land of perpetual famine, a 
land of biggest desert in the country, a land that is more backward than 
Vidarbha, but still farmers do not commit suicide there. They do not have per 
capita income more than Punjab; they do not have per capita income more 
than Tamil Nadu or more than any other Southern State.   But still they have 
learnt to live with frugality.   They have

SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK (Goa): Sir, I stand here to 
support his Bill. One of the criticis ms which has been levelled against the 
Finance Minister is that the present Budget is an uneventful Budget. They say 
so. Perhaps, it is so in one way. In one way it is so because the Budget was 
so nicely crafted that there was hardly any scope for any 
317 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2006] 
criticism. When a Budget is presented, if there is a scope for criticism, there is 
an all-round criticism, all over the co untry and that becomes an event. This 
time, it was not an eventful Budget becaus e it is very good, nicely crafted and 
everyman in the street has accepted this. That is it. Sir, actually, this Budget 
has put the country in top gear and the Opposition out of gear. And, that is 
why, there is envy. They are jealous of this Budget and hence the criticism. I 
will not analyse the Budget, as I don't have time. I am satisfied with various 
allocations, by and large, given to every sector.   I would restrict myself to 
some of the suggestions. 
Sir, as far as Employment Guarantee Scheme is concerned, 
sometimes States like Goa get punish ed because you say that your literacy 
rate is high, you are elite and all those things. Therefore, we are not included. 
Now, Sir, in Goa, the position is lik e this. There for Rs. 150 you can get a 
labour at any time. But, non-manual jobs for young girls and boys, people are 
ready to work even for Rs. 50 a day. Therefore, some scheme has to be 
worked out for this class of people, who are in lakhs and lakhs in a State like 
Goa. Therefore, some amendment has  to be made in the Employment 
Guarantee Scheme for this class of people. 
As far as IT sector is concerne d, I congratulate you, Mr. Deputy 
Chairman, Sir, because you have provided wi-fi connectivity. You have made 
us IT-conscious. In this field also, the Fi nance Minister has laid a lot of stress. 
But, the question is we have to practically implement the IT policy in every 
nook and corner of the country. Finance does not matter. Even with few crores 
of rupees, if proper implementation is there, IT sector can be taken to villages. 
For example, all the orders of the Gove rnment, notifications, tenders, all the 
schemes are made available in the villages, in small kiosks, then, IT sector will 
obviously get flourished, the common man will get the benefits of the IT 
sector. Therefore, it is in the implement ation of the IT sect or that this whole 
matter lies, not in finance as such. Even if finance is comparatively less, and if 
the administrative implementation is better, then, the effect will be more. 
Then, I will come to the National Highways. The question is not, 
again I am saying, of funds. But, what  has been provided to the Ministry, I 
think, the Finance Minister should use his good offices with his colleagues, 
who come from the same State, to give  Goa something. For the last several 
years, we have not been able to bring a small stretch of highway in Goa to the 
standards of National Highways. Now, there is a proposal from Paden to 
Polen in Goa.   I expect that it should be accepted, Directions

[10 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
should be given to the Ministry concerned to provide necessary funds for the 
purpose of upgrading this National Highway in Goa. 
Sir, as far as the Rural Health Mission is concerned, rural health 
centres and district hospitals should be standardised. Standard norms should 
be fixed. Today, in one of the discussions , we came to know that even in the 
matter of cleanliness, we were far, fa r behind. Therefore, whatever money is 
allocated to the health sector, that should be utilised. 
Again, I am pointing out to an issue, which relates to all of us. As far 
as the Central Government Health Services are concerned, there is a talk that 
it is going to be scrapped. We don't know what is going on. If this whole 
scheme is going to be dropped, then what is going to come in its place? I am 
not sure about it. But presuming that it is going to continue, it should be 
ensured that whatever agreements t hat the CGHS aut horities or the 
Government of India has with private hospitals should be made in time. When 
the contract expires, the beneficiaries  and their family members will be in 
trouble because of some gap between one  agreement and another, and they 
have to pay hundreds and thousands of rupees. I think this matter should be 
looked into by the Finance Ministry. 
Another point is about Central Exci se Duty. In February, 2005, the 
hon. Finance Minister taxed the pharmaceutical industry with 16 per cent tax 
on MRP, which actually, according to them, became 30 per cent to 
consumers. Various associations have made representations to bring down 
the Central Excise Duty from 16 per cent  to 8 per cent not only to get a level 
playing field but also with a view to make drugs cheaper and affordable to 
consumers. Sir, if it is  not done, a number of industr ies in the SSI sector in 
Goa will suffer, and they will not be able to survive as they are manufacturing 
products of large companies on contra ct or loan-licence basis, and these 
multinational companies will obviously transfer their business to Himachal 
Pradesh or Uttaranchal in order to take an advantage of tax sop given to them 
which was taken away from us. This aspect has to be looked into. 
Sir, riots, etc., at various places take place over land issues.

aspect is dealt with, there would be less number of quarrels. Small quarrels

defective land reforms.  It has to be tackled with.

SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA (Karnataka): Sir, at the outset, I 
would like to congratulate the hon. Fi nance Minister, Mr. Chidambaramji, for 
presenting a fine, well-balanced, and innovative Budget which has taken care 
of every section of the so ciety. Sir, with business confidence at an all time 
high and economic growth broad based, revenue performance in the last two 
years has been very good. In spite of increase in international oil prices vis-a-
vis indigenous price of petroleum products, inflation has remained low. The 
economy has been managed very well and for this all rewards go to the hon. 
Prime Minister, Dr. Manmohan Singhji. The Budget has set a step further in 
achieving the objectives of growth, stability and equality spelt out in our 
National Common Minimum Programme. 
320 

[10 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
We are maintaining a growth rate of seven to eight per cent per 
annum. The growth rate, which was 7.5 per cent in 2004-05, has increased to 
8.1 per cent in 2005-06. Promoting investment, accelerating fiscal 
consolidation, focussing on agriculture and industries with employment 
potential infrastructure both in rural and  urban areas are the key objectives of 
the Budget. The thrust is mainly on agriculture and rural development through 
Bharat Nirman and several flagship schemes and programmes like Sarva 
Shiksha Abhiyan, Mid-day Meal Scheme, Rajiv Gandhi Drinking Water Mission, 
total sanitation campaign, National Health Mission and Integrated Child 
Development Programme. These schemes are targeted towards the rural 
masses. 
Sir, the budgetary support for Bharat Nirman has been increased by 
54 per cent; likewise, for education, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, one lakh fifty 
thousand additional teachers and five lakh additional class rooms under Sarva 
Shiksha Abhiyan. This should be appreciated. Likewise, the increment in Rajiv 
Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission, rural sanitation campaign, Rural 
Health Mission - all these have to be a ppreciated. Also, the old-age pension, 
where Rs.430 crores is kept. Sir, the old ladies and the old people who were 
getting Rs.75 per month are not benefit ed and are getting Rs.200 per month. 
Short-term credit is provided at seven per cent interest. All these have been 
appreciated by each and every one in the country. 
Sir, assured irrigation, credit dive rsification and creating market for 
agriculture products are the thrust areas so far as agricultural sector is 
concerned. What is important is to ensure that the benefits of various schemes 
and programmes reach the small and marginal farmers. 
The Finance Minister has rightly id entified industries for providing 
incentives, which have employment potentia l. Here, Sir, it is important that 
higher rate of growth in GDP spread by growth in industrial sector should 
generate employment. It should be em ployment-oriented growth. Rs.11,700 
crores to be spent to create rural employment under the National Rural 
Employment Guarantee Scheme. 
The Budget has rightly placed its em phasis on infrastructure sector. 
With a developed infrastructure sector we can attract more foreign direct 
investment.  This has to be appreciated. 
The Finance Minister has opted for significant tax reforms. These 
have helped in not only raising tax revenue but also helped in increasing 
321 

RAJYA SABHA [10 March, 2006] 
tax-GDP ratio.   Indirect tax has declined and direct taxes have increased. All 
these are positive features. 
Sir, another novel feature which is going to help us, is Gender-
Budgeting. Sir, in this, there is a ne ed to provide more funds under various 
women-oriented schemes so as to empower women. 
Sir, I don't want to take more time. You have already told me. Sir, to 
conclude, I must say that this Budget is  growth-oriented and will surely boost 
the economy of our country.   Thank you, Sir.
